canopy.source: Vachellia (Acacia) tortilis, umbrella thorn, flat-topped icon of East African savanna, 4-14 m — Wikipedia / Kew

traits.native_range: Vachellia (Acacia) tortilis, umbrella thorn, flat-topped icon of East African savanna, 4-14 m — Wikipedia / Kew
traits.leaf_shape: compound or lobed leaves in a flat spreading crown
traits.trunk: single trunk, flat-topped crown or, for herbs, a huge single leaf on a stalk
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: flat-topped disc on bare thorny limbs

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two oval cotyledons, then tiny feathery bipinnate leaves on a thin stem with paired spines, some long, straight and white, others short and hooked. The taproot dives deep first. Browsed saplings become dense, low, cage-like spiny bushes for years; once a leader escapes browsers it gains about 1.5 m in two years and only later spreads the flat umbrella crown.
growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Acacia tortilis): up to 21 m, about 1.5 m in 2 years, a 6-7-year-old tree yields 5-6 kg of clean seed, 10-12 kg pods a year at 10 yr; Andersen & Krzywinski 2007 (BMC Ecology): radiocarbon ages of 200-650 yr for trees in Egypt's Eastern Desert, radial growth up to 2.4 mm a year. Germination and height curve estimated.

fruiting.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Acacia tortilis): white or pale yellowish-white heads 0.5-1.1 cm, pods 7-10 cm by 6-10 mm, spirally twisted, 10-12 kg pods per 10-yr tree; the Turkana make porridge from the pods, the Maasai eat immature seeds; Wikipedia: aromatic flowers, springlike coiled pods. Flowering at the onset of the rains, ripening, pod fall and rot times estimated.

traits.native_range: Adansonia digitata, African baobab, scattered giant of sub-Saharan savanna, 8-25 m — Wikipedia

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: huge grey bottle trunk, sparse root-like crown

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling has broad cotyledons and simple, undivided first leaves; hand-shaped leaves with 3, then 5-7 leaflets come later. Young baobabs look nothing like adults: a slender, straight, tapering grey-green whip over a swollen tuberous taproot, with thin branches; the huge bottle trunk and wide crown form only after decades. Seeds are hard and germinate slowly unless scarified.
growth.source: Ethiopian Forestry Dev. baobab study (simple juvenile leaves, 5-7-foliate adult leaves, trees over 1000 yr); Anjarwalla et al. 2021 bioRxiv (seed-grown trees first flower at 8-23 yr; acid-treated seed sprouts in ~5 d); Patrut et al. 2018 Nature Plants (radiocarbon ages to ~2500 yr); height curve estimated

fruiting.source: Venter & Witkowski 2019 For Ecol Manage (southern Africa: flowering 1-5 months peaking Nov, 290-710 flowers per tree, fruit set ~20%); EFD Ethiopia study (57-157 fruits/tree in Benin, 77 in South Africa); Baum 1995 (pendent white flowers open at dusk for one night, fruit-bat pollination)

canopy.silhouette: low twisted tree, thick dark corky bark

growth.juvenile_note: Germination is slow and erratic (months to over a year) from the spiny woody stone. Like many cerrado trees the seedling puts its effort into a deep thick root first and shows only a short stem with a few trifoliate leaves of three broad toothed leaflets; it resprouts after fire and slowly becomes a crooked, thick-barked small tree.
growth.source: Wikipedia/Kew (to 10 m, flowers Jul-Sep in the dry season, bat-pollinated with hummingbird, bee and moth visitors, orange-sized fruit with 1-4 spiny pyrenes, ~5-6 months to ripen, slow germination); Zardo & Henriques 2011 (growth and fruit output in cerrado); growth rates estimated

fruiting.source: Wikipedia Caryocar brasiliense (yellowish-white many-stamened flowers, often two dozen per cluster, bats main pollinators; fruit orange-sized, dark purple to olive to buff green, 1-4 spiny pits; mesocarp eaten mostly cooked with rice); Gribel & Hay 1993 J. Trop. Ecol. (nocturnal one-night flowers); fruit falls when ripe

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: tall straight stringy trunk, thin open crown

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings have opposite, broad lance-shaped stalked leaves (13-15 cm) for several nodes; juvenile leaves are huge (15-35 cm), pendulous and dull blue-green. A woody lignotuber forms early and root suckers arise; in the fire-swept savanna young plants live for years as clumps of leafy resprouts in the grass until fire-free years let one whip-like shoot escape.
growth.source: EUCLID Eucalypts of Australia (E. tetrodonta: seedling and juvenile leaves, lignotuber, adventitious shoots on lateral roots, tree to 25 m); savanna recruitment-bottleneck studies in Kakadu/Munmarlary (Werner, Prior, Bowman). Growth rates and ages estimated.

fruiting.source: EUCLID (flowers Jun-Sep, also Apr-May in the Top End; whitish-cream; buds 3 per umbel; capsule cylindrical 1.2-2 x 0.9-1.4 cm with four small teeth). Pollinators (honeyeaters, flying foxes, bees), ripening to early-wet-season seed fall, fruit set and crop estimated.

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: tall dark straight trunk with round fan crown

growth.juvenile_note: Remote germination: from the big fibrous seed a stout 'sinker' tube burrows up to a metre down, where the embryo forms a starchy tuber (sold as palmyra sprouts). Months later the first leaf, a narrow, pleated, undivided blade, spears up away from the seed; for years the young palm is a trunkless clump of stiff grey-green fan leaves on black, saw-edged stalks.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 30 m; slow establishment phase with few leaves a year before a sudden stem; dioecious); palmyra monographs (Kovoor 1983 FAO; Morton 1988 Econ. Bot.) for remote-tubular germination and first flowering at ~12-20 yr; trunk timing and lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (male flowers <1 cm in catkin-like rachillae, female flowers golf-ball sized; fruit 10-18 cm with black husk ripening purple-black, sweet fibrous pulp, tender seeds eaten); palmyra monographs (flowering Jan-Apr in S India, tender fruit at ~3 months, ripe Jul-Sep; ~6-12 bunches, 100-350 fruits a year).

shrub.silhouette: spiral tufts of long leaves on stilt-rooted stems

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings emerge from a woody fruit segment as a stemless, spiralling rosette of stiff, narrow, sword-like leaves with hooked prickles along the edges and midrib. After a few years a slender trunk lifts the tuft; leaves stay in three ranks that twist around the stem like a corkscrew, and old dead leaves hang as a skirt.
growth.source: Wikipedia and Useful Tropical Plants (to 10 m, dioecious, fruit a syncarp of 10-25 woody drupes); NT Government Pandanus sheet (survives hot fires, seeds float along rivers); growth, germination and ages estimated from Pandanus tectorius

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (syncarp of 10-25 segments, green turning orange or red, 5-7 seeds per segment); NT Government (ripe fruit deep orange-red, later brown when kernels are eaten; floating seeds); Useful Tropical Plants (sweet orange pulp); timing estimated from P. tectorius

shrub.name: Australian cycad

growth.juvenile_note: Germination is hypogeal: the big seed sits on the soil while a taproot goes down. The first fronds are short with only a few pairs of narrow leaflets. For about a decade it is a stemless tuft of a few fronds per yearly flush over a swelling underground stem; then a stubby, fire-blackened trunk rises. Resprouts a whole new crown after dry-season fires.
growth.source: LLIFLE Cycas media (trunk usually 2.7-3.5 m, seldom 6 m; slow; seeds need months of after-ripening; refoliates after fire); Ornduff 1991 Bot. Gaz. 152 (C. media size classes, fire every 2-3 yr, beetles and Trigona bees at cones); Univ. Hamburg cycad seed guide. Growth rates estimated.

shrub.source: N Australian savanna; fire-resprouting.  Kew POWO.

shrub.name: Savanna bamboo
shrub.source: Oxytenanthera abyssinica, African lowland/savanna bamboo, clumps in seasonally dry African savanna woodland, 5-12 m — Wikipedia / PROTA

traits.native_range: Oxytenanthera abyssinica, African lowland/savanna bamboo, clumps in seasonally dry African savanna woodland, 5-12 m — Wi

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: open clump of thin arching culms

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are grassy tufts of thin tillers with lance-shaped leaves, well developed in 4 months. Each rainy season the young clump sends up taller, thicker culms: early ones pencil-thin (about 1 cm) and 2-3 m tall, arching; mature culms are almost solid, 5-10 cm thick, in a dense clump. It flowers once, after 7-21 years, then the clump dies.
growth.source: SANBI PlantZAfrica (seed germinates in 11 days-2 weeks in the rains, shoots well developed in 4 months; young culms 2-3 m x 12 mm; clump matures in 3 yr (Congo) to 8 yr (Zambia); mass flowering after 7-21 years, then the clump dies; culms to 16 m); ICRAF Useful Trees; culm elongation time estimated

shrub.name: Whistling thorn

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two oval cotyledons and small feathery bipinnate leaves on a wiry stem armed with paired straight white spines. Saplings in the black-clay grasslands are browsed and burned back, staying spiny multi-stemmed bushes for years; then they start making swollen hollow thorn bases (bulbs, soft and green at first, hardening purple-black, then grey) that ants move into.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Vachellia drepanolobium): up to 6 m, on East African black-cotton soils, hollow swollen thorns housing Crematogaster and Tetraponera ants (C. mimosae on about half the trees). Germination, growth, first flowering and lifespan estimated from related East African savanna acacias.

shrub.source: East African black-cotton savanna; ant galls. Kew POWO (African acacias are now Vachellia/Senegalia; Acacia is the Australian wattles). Thorny (African), flat crowns, insect-pollinated, pods eaten by browsers which spread the seed; giraffe and goat browse; fire-adapted.

ground.silhouette: tendril climber with red-yellow flame flowers

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings come up slowly and erratically (1-6 months); the first season often makes only a short unbranched shoot with a few glossy lance-shaped leaves and a pea-sized tuber. Each year the finger-like tuber grows and forks, sending up a longer, weak stem that climbs by tendril-like leaf tips through shrubs, then dies back to the tuber in the dry season.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Gloriosa superba: climbing stems to 4 m from a fleshy tuberous rhizome; highly toxic, colchicine). Germination time, tuber-building years and ages estimated from Gloriosa cultivation.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (solitary flowers with 6 reflexed wavy tepals 5-7.6 cm, red to orange with yellowish bases; likely pollinated by butterflies and sunbirds; fleshy capsule 6-12 cm with red seeds; all parts poisonous). Monsoon season, timings and counts estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are thin, bright-green grass tufts that establish slowly (about 6 months before they can be grazed, up to 2 years to a full stand). They grow into a dense tussock of tall, coarse culms that turn rusty red as the loose, feathery panicles of paired, awned spikelets ripen at the end of the rains; burnt tussocks resprout from the base.
growth.source: Feedipedia (Hyparrhenia rufa: robust densely tufted perennial 60-240 cm, slow establishment ~6 months to 2 years, fast-growing once established, regrows after fire, no frost); germination, first seed and lifespan estimated.
